title: How Government Learns: Building the Feedback Loop
description:
This introductory session provides a practical overview of how state and local governments can move beyond compliance-oriented reporting toward more adaptive and learning-oriented approaches to program management. Participants will explore how program evaluation, performance management, continuous improvement, adaptive management, and organizational learning fit together to support more effective public-sector decision-making.

The session also introduces practical uses of AI tools to help agencies organize information, identify patterns, summarize findings, support reporting, and improve organizational learning while maintaining transparency and ethical safeguards.
learning_goals:
• Understand the relationship between program evaluation, continuous improvement, adaptive management, and organizational learning.

  • Recognize how agencies can demonstrate ongoing program value and effectiveness to multiple stakeholders.

  • Identify practical ways AI tools can support evidence-informed decision-making and organizational learning.

title: How Government Acts: Putting Data to Work
description:
This moderated discussion focuses on how state and local agencies use quantitative information to monitor implementation, assess effectiveness, identify challenges, demonstrate program worthiness, and adapt programs over time. Speakers will discuss practical lessons learned from using dashboards, indicators, operational metrics, and AI-supported analytical tools to improve programs and public services in areas such as transportation, workforce development, housing, public health, infrastructure, and economic development.

The session also explores organizational challenges involving staff capacity, data quality, transparency, procurement, and public trust.
learning_goals:
• Understand how agencies use operational and program data to support continuous improvement and adaptive management.

  • Learn how AI tools can support data organization, visualization, analysis, and reporting.

  • Recognize how governments communicate the impact and ongoing value of programs to decision-makers and the public.

title: How Government Adapts: Learning from Community Experience
description:
This moderated discussion examines how governments use interviews, focus groups, community listening sessions, observations, case studies, and stakeholder engagement to better understand program performance, community experiences, and implementation challenges. Speakers will discuss how qualitative information supports adaptive management, strengthens public trust, demonstrates community value, and improves government responsiveness.

The session also explores practical uses of AI tools to assist with transcription, coding, theme extraction, summarization, and synthesis of public feedback while maintaining ethical and transparent evaluation practices.
learning_goals:
• Understand the role of qualitative information in continuous improvement and adaptive management.

  • Identify practical approaches for incorporating community feedback into program management and decision-making.

  • Learn how AI tools can support qualitative analysis and synthesis while maintaining human judgment and transparency.

title: Prompting Lab: The Elements of a Good Prompt
description:
Getting useful results from generative AI starts with knowing how to ask the right question. For public professionals who are new to AI tools, prompting can feel like guesswork: What information should you include? How much context is enough? How do you ask for the tone, format, or level of detail you need?

In this beginner-friendly Prompting Lab, you will learn the basic structure of an effective prompt and practice building prompts that support everyday public sector work. We will break down key elements such as context, task, role, audience, tone, format, examples, and constraints. Through practical exercises, you will learn how to move from a vague request to a clearer, more useful prompt that keeps human judgment, accuracy, and accountability at the center.

This workshop is designed for public professionals who are starting to use generative AI and want a practical, low-pressure introduction to prompting.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify the core elements of a strong prompt, including context, task, role, tone, audience, format, and constraints.
  • Apply a simple prompt structure to common public sector tasks such as drafting, summarizing, planning, and simplifying information.
  • Revise vague prompts to make them clearer, more specific, and better aligned with the intended outcome.
  • Evaluate AI-generated responses for usefulness, accuracy, tone, and fit for public sector work.
  • Use prompting practices that support transparency, human oversight, and responsible use of AI.

title: The Prompting Lab Office Hours: Bring Your AI Questions
description:
After learning the basics of prompt structure, the next step is practice. This follow-up office hours session gives you a chance to bring your questions, test prompts, troubleshoot challenges, and learn from peers who are also beginning to use generative AI in their work.
Led as an interactive, peer-to-peer session, this office hours workshop will help you refine prompts for real public sector tasks, from drafting emails and summarizing documents to preparing meeting materials, translating complex ideas into plain language, or organizing information. You will have space to ask what is working, what is not, and how to improve your prompts while keeping accuracy, judgment, privacy, and accountability in mind.
This session is designed for public professionals who attended the introductory Prompting Lab or who already understand the basic elements of a prompt and want guided practice
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Improve prompts based on feedback, examples, and peer discussion.
  • Troubleshoot common prompting challenges, including unclear outputs, wrong tone, missing context, or overly broad responses.
  • Adapt prompt structures to fit different public sector tasks and audiences.
  • Assess when an AI-generated response needs revision, verification, or additional human judgment.
  • Share practical prompting approaches that can be applied in day-to-day government work.

title: AI Changes: Buy vs. Build
description:
AI is changing the choices public agencies face when planning new technology. Work that once required lengthy procurements or expensive custom software can now sometimes be prototyped, tested, or improved by public-sector teams using generative and agentic AI.

In this workshop, you will explore how AI is changing the economics of government technology and what that means for buy-versus-build decisions. You will learn how to assess when to purchase commercial tools, when to build internally, and when to combine both approaches to create services that are sustainable, accountable, and valuable to the public.
short_description: Explore how AI is changing the economics of government technology and what that means for buy-versus-build decisions. You will learn how to assess when to purchase commercial tools, when to build internally, and when to combine both approaches to create services that are sustainable, accountable, and valuable to the public.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Assess how generative and agentic AI are changing buy-versus-build decisions in government.
  • Identify when to buy, build, or combine commercial and internally developed solutions.
  • Evaluate tradeoffs around cost, speed, sustainability, accountability, and public value.

title: From Projects to Products
description:
Too often, government technology work is organized around one-time projects: launch a system, close the contract, and move on. But residents’ needs, policy requirements, and service conditions continue to change after launch.

In this workshop, you will explore how public agencies can shift toward a product mindset focused on continuous improvement, user needs, and measurable public outcomes. You will learn what product management looks like in government and how teams can use feedback, data, and iteration to build services that keep improving over time.
short_description: Explore how public agencies can shift toward a product mindset focused on continuous improvement, user needs, and measurable public outcomes. You will learn what product management looks like in government and how teams can use feedback, data, and iteration to build services that keep improving over time.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Distinguish between project-based and product-based approaches to government technology.
  • Apply a product mindset centered on user needs, continuous improvement, and public outcomes.
  • Identify practices teams can use to prioritize, measure, and improve digital services over time.

title: The Rise of the Citizen Developer
description:
AI is expanding who can help build and improve government services. Policy experts, analysts, program managers, and frontline staff can now use AI-enabled tools to prototype applications, automate routine workflows, and solve operational problems that once required specialized technical support.

In this workshop, you will explore how public agencies can support citizen developers while maintaining the governance, training, and oversight needed to innovate responsibly. You will learn how AI fellowships, internal support models, and cross-functional collaboration can help agencies turn staff expertise into practical service improvements.
short_description:
AI is expanding who can help build and improve government services. Policy experts, analysts, program managers, and frontline staff can now use AI-enabled tools to prototype applications, automate routine workflows, and solve operational problems that once required specialized technical support.

In this workshop, you will explore how public agencies can support citizen developers while maintaining the governance, training, and oversight needed to innovate responsibly. You will learn how AI fellowships, internal support models, and cross-functional collaboration can help agencies turn staff expertise into practical service improvements.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify opportunities for nontechnical staff to use AI-enabled tools to improve workflows and services.
  • Apply governance and support practices that help citizen developers innovate responsibly.
  • Evaluate training, fellowship, and collaboration models that build internal AI capacity.

title: Building High-Performing Product Teams
description:
AI-enabled services are not built by technology teams alone. Strong public-sector products require collaboration across product, design, engineering, procurement, policy, legal, program, and service delivery teams — each bringing knowledge that helps ensure the product is useful, responsible, and sustainable.

In this workshop, you will explore how high-performing product teams work in government. You will learn how different roles can collaborate across the product lifecycle, from defining the problem and setting priorities to managing risks, governing AI use, and improving services over time.
short_description:
AI-enabled services are not built by technology teams alone. Strong public-sector products require collaboration across product, design, engineering, procurement, policy, legal, program, and service delivery teams — each bringing knowledge that helps ensure the product is useful, responsible, and sustainable.

In this workshop, you will explore how high-performing product teams work in government. You will learn how different roles can collaborate across the product lifecycle, from defining the problem and setting priorities to managing risks, governing AI use, and improving services over time.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify the roles and skills needed to build and manage AI-enabled public-sector products.
  • Apply collaboration practices that help product, technical, policy, legal, and program teams work together effectively.
  • Evaluate governance and operating models that support responsible product development over time.

title: Scaling Government Innovation
description:
Many public agencies are experimenting with AI, but the harder work begins after a promising pilot. To create lasting public value, governments need ways to measure impact, sustain digital services, share what works, and build the internal capacity to keep improving over time.

In this workshop, you will explore how agencies can move from individual pilots to durable institutional capability. You will learn practical approaches for evaluating results, maintaining AI-enabled products, reusing solutions across agencies, and creating the culture and operating models needed to make innovation sustainable.
short_description:
Many public agencies are experimenting with AI, but the harder work begins after a promising pilot. To create lasting public value, governments need ways to measure impact, sustain digital services, share what works, and build the internal capacity to keep improving over time.

In this workshop, you will explore how agencies can move from individual pilots to durable institutional capability. You will learn practical approaches for evaluating results, maintaining AI-enabled products, reusing solutions across agencies, and creating the culture and operating models needed to make innovation sustainable.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Measure the impact of AI-enabled pilots using outcomes tied to service quality, efficiency, and public value.
  • Identify practices for maintaining, adapting, and sharing reusable digital products across agencies.
  • Develop strategies to build a sustainable culture of innovation and continuous improvement in government.

title: Why Measuring AI Is Hard
description:
AI systems routinely achieve impressive scores on standardized tests and benchmarks, yet those results often tell us little about whether a tool will succeed in a real government setting.
This session explores the limitations of common AI benchmarks, the differences between predictive and generative AI systems, and why performance in laboratory tests often fails to predict success in real-world settings.
short_description: Explore the limitations of common AI benchmarks, the differences between predictive and generative AI systems, and why performance in laboratory tests often fails to predict success in real-world settings.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Explain why standard AI benchmarks and test scores may not predict how well an AI system will perform on real government tasks and workflows.
  • Distinguish key evaluation challenges for predictive and generative AI systems and identify why each requires different approaches to measuring performance.
  • Identify the factors agencies should consider when defining meaningful measures of AI effectiveness, reliability, and public value in real-world government settings.

title: Measuring What Matters
description: Many AI evaluations focus on efficiency metrics such as time saved, documents processed, or staff hours reduced. This session examines how agencies can move beyond productivity measures to define success in terms of service quality, accuracy, equity, public trust, resident and worker experience, and public outcomes. Participants will learn practical approaches for identifying meaningful measures of public value.
short_description: This session examines how agencies can move beyond productivity measures to define success in terms of service quality, accuracy, equity, public trust, resident and worker experience, and public outcomes.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Distinguish between efficiency metrics and broader measures of AI effectiveness and public value.
  • Identify meaningful measures of success across service quality, accuracy, equity, public trust, and resident and worker experience.
  • Develop practical measures for evaluating whether AI use is improving public services and contributing to better outcomes.

title: Comparing Humans, AI, and Human-AI Teams
description: The most important question is often not whether AI performs well in isolation, but whether it improves performance relative to current practice. This session explores methods for comparing human-only, AI-only, and human-plus-AI workflows and identifying where AI adds value, where it creates risks, and where hybrid approaches perform best.
short_description: Explore methods for comparing human-only, AI-only, and human-plus-AI workflows and identifying where AI adds value, where it creates risks, and where hybrid approaches perform best.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Compare the performance of human-only, AI-only, and human-plus-AI approaches across real-world government tasks and workflows.
  • Identify where AI can improve current practices, where it may introduce new risks, and where human judgment and oversight remain essential.
  • Evaluate when hybrid human-AI approaches can deliver better performance, reliability, and public outcomes than either humans or AI working alone.

title: Try Before and After You Buy
description: How can agencies assess whether an AI tool is likely to work before committing significant resources? This session covers practical methods for testing AI systems prior to procurement or deployment, including baseline comparisons, pilot design, task-based evaluation, and the identification of acceptable and unacceptable risks. Also, performance can change as models evolve, workflows shift, staff adapt their practices, and systems encounter new contexts and use cases. This session explores how agencies can monitor performance over time, detect emerging problems, and understand when an initially successful implementation may require adjustment or reevaluation.
short_description: This session explores how agencies can monitor performance over time, detect emerging problems, and understand when an initially successful implementation may require adjustment or reevaluation.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Design practical pre-deployment evaluations that compare AI performance against current practices and establish meaningful baselines.
  • Identify acceptable and unacceptable risks through task-based testing and well-designed pilots before committing significant resources to AI adoption.
  • Develop approaches for monitoring AI performance over time and determining when changes in models, workflows, or use cases require adjustment, reevaluation, or retirement.

title: Principles for Public-Sector AI Evaluation
description: Drawing on lessons from research and practice, this session presents a practical framework for evaluating AI in government. Participants will leave with a set of principles, methods, and questions for assessing AI effectiveness, measuring public value, monitoring performance over time, and making informed decisions about adoption, scaling, redesign, or retirement.
short_description: Drawing on lessons from research and practice, this session presents a practical framework for evaluating AI in government.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Apply a practical framework for evaluating AI effectiveness and public value in government settings.
  • Use evidence from testing and ongoing monitoring to assess whether AI systems continue to meet agency needs and performance expectations.
  • Make informed decisions about when to adopt, scale, redesign, or retire an AI system based on performance, risks, and public outcomes.

title: AI, Data Centers, and Growing Resource Demands
description: As governments, utilities, and technology companies expand AI infrastructure, questions are emerging about electricity demand, water use, land use, emissions, transmission capacity, and community impacts. This session examines what is driving AI-related resource demand, what remains uncertain, and how public officials can evaluate competing claims about economic development, sustainability, affordability, and reliability.
short_description: This session examines what is driving AI-related resource demand, what remains uncertain, and how public officials can evaluate competing claims about economic development, sustainability, affordability, and reliability.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify the key drivers of AI-related electricity, water, land, and infrastructure demands.
  • Evaluate competing claims about the economic, environmental, affordability, and reliability impacts of AI infrastructure.
  • Assess the tradeoffs public officials should consider when planning for data center growth and its impacts on communities.

title: Using AI to Improve Energy and Environmental Systems
description: Public agencies, utilities, and environmental organizations are increasingly exploring how AI can support forecasting, grid operations, infrastructure planning, environmental monitoring, resilience, permitting, and resource management. This session examines where these applications are delivering value in practice, where results remain uncertain, and how organizations can assess whether AI is improving outcomes. Participants will explore real-world uses and practical approaches for evaluating performance, effectiveness, and impact.
short_description: Explore how public agencies, utilities, and environmental organizations are using AI across energy and environmental systems, where these applications are delivering value, and how organizations can evaluate their effectiveness and impact.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify practical applications of AI in energy management, environmental monitoring, infrastructure planning, resilience, permitting, and resource management.
  • Evaluate where AI is delivering measurable value and where its benefits remain uncertain or unproven.
  • Apply practical criteria for assessing whether AI-supported approaches can improve energy and environmental outcomes.

title: Policy Choices, Investment Strategies, and Governance
description: Governments face difficult choices as AI-related infrastructure expands and AI becomes more integrated into energy and environmental systems. This session examines policy, regulatory, planning, procurement, and investment approaches being used to manage growth, protect communities, support innovation, maintain grid reliability, and advance environmental goals. Participants will explore the tradeoffs associated with different approaches and the questions public officials should ask before making decisions.
short_description: Explore how governments are using policy, regulation, planning, procurement, and investment to manage AI-related infrastructure growth while balancing innovation, community impacts, grid reliability, and environmental goals.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Compare policy, regulatory, procurement, planning, and investment approaches for managing AI-related infrastructure and applications.
  • Analyze tradeoffs among economic development, community impacts, grid reliability, innovation, affordability, and environmental goals.
  • Identify key questions public officials should ask when making decisions about AI-related infrastructure, investments, and governance.

title: When AI Creates New Risks
description: AI introduces new ways for information to be exposed, manipulated, or misused, while AI systems themselves can create new security and operational vulnerabilities. Using real-world examples, this session examines how AI is changing the security landscape for government, including risks related to data leakage, prompt injection, public-facing AI tools, shadow AI, and other emerging threats. Participants will learn to recognize how seemingly routine uses of AI can create significant security and operational consequences—and what to watch for in their own work.
short_description: Learn to recognize common and emerging cybersecurity risks associated with AI and understand how everyday uses of AI can create security and operational consequences for public agencies.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify common cybersecurity and operational risks associated with the use of AI in government.
  • Recognize how risks such as data leakage, prompt injection, and shadow AI can emerge in everyday work.
  • Assess how routine decisions about using AI tools can create broader risks for their teams and organizations.

title: Evaluating AI Tools and Vendors
description: This session examines the questions public officials should ask before adopting AI-enabled products and services, including how vendors handle data, manage security and access, use information for model training, and respond to security incidents. Participants will learn what to look for when evaluating vendor practices and contractual protections and how to identify potential risks before committing to a tool.
short_description: Learn what questions to ask about data, security, access, vendor practices, and contractual protections before your agency adopts an AI-enabled product or service.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify key security and data protection questions to ask when evaluating AI-enabled products and vendors.
  • Assess vendor practices related to data handling, access permissions, model training, and security incidents.
  • Recognize potential risks and contractual protections to consider before adopting an AI-enabled tool or service.

title: Managing AI Risk Across the Organization
description: This session explores how agencies can develop governance processes, escalation pathways, staff guidance, and cross-functional partnerships to support safer, more responsible AI adoption. Participants will learn how different roles across an organization can contribute to identifying, communicating, and managing AI-related risks.
short_description: Explore how public agencies can manage AI-related risks through clear governance, staff guidance, escalation processes, and collaboration across technical and nontechnical teams.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify how different roles and teams across an agency contribute to managing AI-related cybersecurity risks.
  • Develop practical approaches to staff guidance, governance, and escalation when AI-related risks arise.
  • Strengthen cross-functional collaboration to support safer and more responsible AI adoption across the organization.

title: Getting Started Without Getting Overwhelmed - How procurement teams are taking their first AI steps
description: Learn how procurement teams are taking their first steps with AI without a big budget or a dedicated tech team. Two practitioner stories show how a "start small" approach can turn a routine, time-consuming task into a quick, reliable one, and how a small, resourceful team found its own starting point without extra resources. Walk away with a practical way to identify where AI can support your team's work first.
learning_goals:
• Identify a small, low-risk task in your own procurement process where AI could save time or reduce error

  • Recognize what conditions (data, tools, staff buy-in) make a first AI project more likely to succeed

  • Apply a simple framework for scoping and piloting a first AI use case in your organization

title: AI Across the Procurement Lifecycle — Where Does It Actually Fit?
description: Explore where AI tools fit across the procurement lifecycle, whether planning, solicitation, evaluation, and contract management. See a large-state perspective on integrating AI into a high-volume procurement operation, including where it adds the most value and where human judgement still leads.
learning_goals:
• Map AI tools and use cases to specific stages of the procurement lifecycle

  • Distinguish between tasks well-suited to AI support and those that require continued human judgement

  • Evaluate a demonstrated AI tool for potential fit within your own procurement workflow

title: AI Tools Showcase — What's Out There and How to Evaluate It
description: See how public procurement teams are evaluating AI tools, including contract analytics, RFP drafting assistants, and AI-enabled ERP features, from people who've actually used them.  Hear how municipalities have selected and scoped a tool for its own procurement needs.
learning_goals:
• Apply a set of criteria for evaluating AI procurement tools beyond vendor claims

  • Identify questions to ask vendors about data use, accuracy, and accountability

  • Compare tool features against your organization's specific procurement needs and constraints

title: From Chatbots to Agents
description: AI agents are often described as the next generation of AI, but the reality is more nuanced. Most organizations move gradually from using AI for drafting and research to using AI that remembers context, automates tasks, coordinates workflows, and eventually takes action on a user's behalf. This session explores that evolution and explains how agents differ from chatbots, copilots, workflow automation, and traditional software tools. Drawing on early government examples, participants will learn where agencies are experimenting with agentic capabilities today and how to distinguish meaningful innovation from marketing hype.

title: From Prompts to Workflows
description: Most public professionals use AI one task at a time. Agents offer the possibility of creating reusable workflows that can support recurring work. This session explores how agencies are using agentic workflows for research, communications, permitting, grants management, procurement, case preparation, constituent services, and other operational activities. Participants will learn how to identify workflows that may benefit from agentic approaches and where simpler tools may be sufficient.

title: Bringing Agents to Work
description: Technology adoption is ultimately a people challenge. How do agencies help staff move from occasional AI use to meaningful integration into everyday work? This session examines strategies for workforce adoption, training, change management, experimentation, and learning. Participants will explore how organizations are helping employees identify high-value use cases, redesign workflows, build confidence in agentic tools, and create feedback loops that improve both performance and governance over time.

title: What Works—and What Doesn't
description: Agentic systems create new opportunities but also new risks. Drawing on lessons from early adopters, this session examines what agencies are learning about reliability, privacy and security, human oversight, transparency, accountability, and governance. Participants will leave with practical principles for deciding where agents are appropriate, where safeguards are required, and how to experiment, scale, and govern agentic systems responsibly.

title: The Basics and the Breakthrough Opportunities
description:
Public health is one of the most important—and underdeveloped—frontiers for artificial intelligence. While AI is rapidly reshaping clinical care, its application in public health remains early, fragmented, and full of untapped potential. This session introduces participants to the current state of the field and provides a practical foundation for understanding how AI can support population health goals.

Participants will receive a clear, accessible introduction to core AI concepts and explore how they connect to established public health methods including epidemiology and real-world evidence. The session will examine approaches for developing ethical and responsible AI systems that center human and community agency and discuss how public health leaders can begin building AI literacy and readiness within their organizations.

The workshop will also address why adoption has moved slowly despite growing interest. Participants will explore common barriers—including fragmented data systems, weak cross-agency coordination, institutional risk aversion, and complex governance environments—and leave with a practical understanding of why advancing an AI-enabled public health agenda has become increasingly urgent for improving outcomes and reducing harms such as misinformation and inequitable access.

title: Health Information in the AI Era: Combating Misinformation and Reaching the Public
description:
Public health agencies are entering a new information environment in which artificial intelligence is changing not only how information is created and distributed, but also how residents search for, interpret, and trust health guidance. AI has the potential to accelerate misinformation and deepen confusion—but it also creates new opportunities for public institutions to communicate more effectively and build stronger relationships with communities.

This session explores the evolving landscape of health misinformation and examines how AI can both amplify and counter these dynamics. Participants will discuss approaches for evaluating and monitoring AI-enabled communication systems and consider how public agencies can use these tools responsibly.

The workshop will focus on practical strategies already beginning to emerge across the field, including AI-powered chatbots that provide trusted guidance, community-based information channels and kiosks, and more personalized communication approaches. The goal is to help participants move beyond passive information delivery toward more responsive, adaptive, and trusted forms of public engagement.

title: Benefits Access and Delivery: Using AI to Expand Reach, Simply Systems, and Improve Integrity
description:
Public health outcomes are shaped not only by healthcare, but also by whether residents can successfully access the benefits and supports available to them. Yet public benefits systems remain difficult to navigate, fragmented across agencies, and burdensome for both residents and administrators. This session explores how artificial intelligence can help modernize access while preserving equity, privacy, and public trust.

Participants will examine how AI tools can simplify enrollment and improve service delivery through intelligent assistants, user-centered application experiences, and emerging agentic approaches that support form completion and guide users through complex processes. The session will also explore how AI can help connect traditionally separate systems—aligning health, nutrition, housing, and income supports while identifying eligibility across multiple programs.

And, the workshop will examine how AI can strengthen program integrity and administrative effectiveness through better data coordination, fraud detection, and improved decision support. Throughout, participants will learn more about governance, consent, and implementation questions that agencies must address to ensure these tools expand access rather than create new barriers.

title: Prediction Isn't Judgment: What Predictive AI Can—and Cannot—Do
description: Predictive systems are increasingly used to forecast risks, identify priorities, allocate resources, and support public-sector decision-making. But prediction is not the same as judgment. This session explores how predictive AI works, what different kinds of predictive systems actually predict, and where prediction can improve government performance. Participants will learn how to distinguish between problems that are well-suited to predictive approaches and those that require other forms of analysis, expertise, or public deliberation.

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
description: Some predictive systems have helped governments improve inspections, anticipate service needs, target interventions, and allocate resources more effectively. Others have failed because of poor data, flawed assumptions, feedback loops, bias, or misplaced confidence in uncertain forecasts. Through real-world examples, participants will examine both successful and unsuccessful deployments of predictive AI and learn how to identify common warning signs, limitations, and unintended consequences before they become costly mistakes.

title: Governing Prediction
description: What questions should public professionals ask before adopting a predictive system? How should agencies evaluate performance, monitor outcomes, and maintain accountability when predictive tools are used to inform decisions? This session examines practical approaches to procurement, oversight, transparency, monitoring, and governance. Participants will leave with a framework for ensuring that predictive systems augment rather than replace human judgment and that public-sector decisions remain accountable, explainable, and aligned with public values.

title: AI in Practice: How Public-Sector Lawyers Are Using AI
description: How are government attorneys and legal staff actually using AI today? This session explores practical applications across legal research, drafting, policy analysis, procurement, compliance, public guidance, investigations, discovery, and document review. Participants will examine real-world examples, lessons learned, and strategies for identifying appropriate use cases within their own organizations.

title: AI and Legal Ethics in Public Service
description: How do professional responsibility obligations apply when AI is used in legal practice? This session explores competence, confidentiality, supervision, transparency, accountability, and the continuing role of human judgment. Participants will examine emerging guidance from bar associations, government agencies, and legal organizations and discuss how public-sector obligations may differ from private-sector practice.

title: Building and Buying Legal AI
description: The market for legal AI tools is expanding rapidly. At the same time, many organizations are creating their own custom assistants, knowledge systems, and workflow tools. This session examines how public-sector legal offices can evaluate, procure, configure, and govern AI systems. Participants will learn what questions to ask vendors, when custom solutions may make sense, and how to design safeguards that support responsible adoption.

title: How Governments Are Buying AI Now
description: Governments and public bodies have many ways of acquiring AI tools: enterprise licenses, pilots, features embedded in software they already use, and heavily discounted offers built for the public sector. Each path solves some problems while carrying consequences for cost, flexibility, and the degree of control a government keeps over its own systems and data. This session maps how AI is entering public institutions today and what those acquisition choices set in motion. Participants will look at the patterns that shape this market, including deep discounting, centralized purchasing, closed ecosystems, and the unmanaged adoption of tools by staff, and consider how different options can either narrow or improve the future delivery of public services and government operations.
learning_goals:
• Understand the ways AI is currently acquired and used in government. 

  • Recognize how common acquisition choices affect cost, flexibility, and control over data, models, and workflows.

  • Identify where governments retain leverage to shape what they buy rather than accept default terms.

  • Assess how a current or recent AI acquisition in their own context is likely to shape their options going forward.

title: What is Public and Democratic AI and Why it Matters
description: A growing set of efforts argues that the public should have a more direct stake in how AI systems are built and overseen. This idea travels under several names, public AI and democratic AI among them. At its core, this idea calls for greater public involvement in AI, more transparency and accountability in how those systems operate, and infrastructure that is open and shared rather than controlled by a single vendor. This session works through what these features mean on a practical level and why proponents believe they produce systems that are both more accountable and more capable. The goal is to give participants a clear and critical understanding of what public and democratic AI offers, what it asks of the government, and why the distinction from a purely commercial approach matters for their work.
learning_goals:
• Understand what public and democratic AI means in practice.

  • Understand the arguments for and against a greater public role in AI.

  • Connect these ideas to the concrete decisions about building, buying, governing, and using AI that participants face in their own work.

title: Putting Public and Democratic AI into Practice
description: This closing session looks at concrete examples of how public institutions have used, built, or bought AI in ways that keep meaningful control in public hands. Participants will examine the choices that made these efforts work, what they required in money, skill, and political support, and the points where they ran into trouble or fell short. The emphasis is on how a given approach succeeded under particular conditions and what a public servant working under different constraints can reasonably take away. By the end, participants will be able to recognize where the openings for public and democratic AI exist in their own institutions and what it would take to act on them.
learning_goals:
• Understand how public institutions have harnessed AI in ways that preserve public control while delivering results.

  • Recognize the conditions that allowed these efforts to work.

  • Learn from where these efforts struggled or fell short.

  • Identify realistic openings to apply public and democratic AI approaches in participants’ own work.

title: Communicating in a Fragmented Media Landscape: Reaching Audiences Across Platforms and Echo Chambers
description:
A press release, a press conference, the local paper, a public meeting. That used to be the whole job. Now your residents are split across newsletters, podcasts, group chats, and short-form video, sorted by algorithms into audiences that never overlap, and a growing number ask ChatGPT about government services instead of visiting your website. What the AI says about your agency is your communication, whether you wrote it or not. This session covers how to show up across a fractured landscape without fracturing your message: adapting to each platform while sounding like one credible voice, reaching low-trust and ideologically distinct communities, and getting your content found when the searcher is a language model.

Participants will leave with:

  • A clearer picture of today's fragmented media landscape and what it means for public sector outreach

  • Practical frameworks for adapting messages across platforms while maintaining a consistent, trustworthy voice

  • Strategies for reaching audiences in echo chambers and low-trust information environments

  • Tools for using audience data and platform analytics to inform — not replace — human communication decisions

title: Explaining AI: How Communicators Can Explain What Their Agency Is Doing with AI
description:
Your agency is probably already using AI to process applications, flag fraud, or route services. Most residents don't know. When they find out, they'll have three questions: Who's accountable? Can it be wrong? What happens to my data? The communicators who can answer plainly will build trust. The ones who reach for jargon or evasion will spend years rebuilding it. What does the public actually want to know about government AI, how to explain algorithmic decisions without a computer science degree on either end, and what to say when the system gets it wrong. Because it will, and your answer for that day should already exist.

Participants will leave with:

  • A working understanding of how government AI systems operate and where they are most commonly deployed

  • Frameworks for explaining algorithmic decision-making to non-technical audiences in plain, credible language

  • Strategies for communicating accountability, oversight, and human review in AI-assisted processes

  • Practical messaging approaches for common scenarios, including service delivery, benefits, and law enforcement applications

title: Communicating Across Language and Cultural Barriers: Equity, Access, and Multilingual Outreach
description:
A five-person comms team can now do things in twelve languages that used to require twelve contractors. That's the opportunity. The risk is doing it badly: machine-translated documents with no cultural context, sent into communities where trust was already thin. This session is the difference. We'll build a real multilingual workflow live, with AI doing the volume and humans doing the judgment, and cover the partnership strategies that make translated outreach land as intended rather than as an afterthought.

Participants will leave with:

  • A framework for assessing whether their agency's communications are equitably reaching all constituents

  • Practical plain-language and culturally responsive design principles that improve clarity for all audiences

  • Strategies for building community partnerships that support authentic, trusted outreach to underserved populations

  • A clear-eyed understanding of when and how to use AI translation and localization tools — and when human expertise must guide the work

title: Workforce Planning, Job Design, and Skills-Based Hiring
description: Good hiring starts with a clear picture of how people can contribute and grow within the organization.   Understanding the skills and capability development that an agency needs now and in the future shapes everything from job classifications to job design to AI execution of routine tasks. This session explores how AI can help HR teams analyze staffing needs, identify skill gaps, and review outdated job classifications. It also looks at how AI can support skills-based hiring by clarifying core competencies and reconsidering unnecessary degree requirements. Participants will hear early lessons from a state-based project and discuss what it takes to open the door to a wider talent pool without lowering the bar on the achievement of critical outcomes.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Describe at least two ways AI can help analyze staffing needs, identify skill gaps, or flag outdated job classifications.

  • Explain what skills-based hiring means in practice, including how clarifying core competencies can reduce reliance on unnecessary degree requirements.

  • Name key takeaways from a public sector project that they could apply when starting a similar effort in their own agency.

title: Recruiting, Onboarding, Learning, and Performance
description: Finding the right person for the right job depends on getting the word out, cultivating interest, making it easy to apply, identifying the right candidate, and then bringing them onboard and supporting their learning to achieve breakthrough performance. No area of the HR function is more exposed to workflow redesign through AI than these functions. The stakes for getting these core functions right could not be higher. An employee’s first weeks, and the chances they get to grow afterward, shape whether they stay in public service. This session looks at how AI has been deployed to create clearer, better outcomes at each stage of the process that links recruiting to outcomes, including how AI can make performance reviews more consistent, timely, and useful for both managers and employees. We will also look at AI mistakes and problems, including bias, failures of judgement, inflexibility, and privacy breaches. Join this session to learn how to achieve greater effectiveness and efficiency in core personnel development functions – and how to avoid the pitfalls.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify where AI is currently used across the recruiting-to-performance pipeline, from job postings and candidate screening to onboarding, learning support, and performance reviews.

  • Describe how AI can support a fairer, more useful performance review process, and where human judgment must remain central.

  • List practical questions to ask before adopting or expanding an AI tool for recruiting, onboarding, or performance management.

title: Pay, Benefits, and Workplace Wellbeing
description: Compensation and benefits administration involves high-volume, detail-heavy work where errors directly affect people’s lives. This session explores how AI could help HR teams spot pay inequities, reduce administrative burden, and help employees understand their benefits. It covers why decisions about individual pay and eligibility require judgement that demands humans in the loop.  Challenges include supporting employee wellbeing without crossing a line into surveillance; how to sustain compassion and human connection supported by AI; and how to understand well-being at a deeper and more substantial leve.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Describe how AI can help flag potential pay inequities and reduce administrative burden in compensation and benefits work.

  • Distinguish between tasks AI can reasonably support and decisions about individual pay and eligibility that require a human in the loop.

  • Recognize the line between using AI to support employee wellbeing and using it in ways that feel like surveillance.

title: Talking to Your Workers: Trust Before Technology
description: Before an agency chooses a tool, vendor, or rollout timeline, it needs to have an honest conversation with the people who will actually use the technology. This opening workshop focuses on how public sector managers can approach those conversations — not as a one-time announcement, but as an ongoing dialogue that builds trust rather than anxiety. Speakers from government and organized labor will share what it looks like to talk openly with workers about what AI adoption means for their jobs, their expertise, and their rights, and why starting with trust — rather than a finished plan — leads to better outcomes for everyone involved.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Recognize why early, honest communication with workers changes the trajectory of AI adoption.

  • Identify common sources of worker anxiety around AI and practical ways managers can address them directly.

  • Describe approaches for talking transparently about job impact, worker expertise, and legal rights before technology decisions are finalized.

title: Governance With Workers: Building Joint Frameworks
description: Trust-building conversations are a starting point — but lasting change requires structure. This workshop looks at how public agencies and their unions have moved beyond one-off conversations to build joint governance frameworks that give workers a real, ongoing role in shaping AI policy. Drawing on real examples, speakers will discuss what it takes to design governance structures, including policies, standards, and guardrails, where power over AI decisions is genuinely shared between management and labor.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Understand what joint governance structures for workplace AI can look like in practice.

  • Identify the legal and contractual mechanisms unions and agencies have used to formalize worker input on AI policy.

  • Apply lessons from cities that have negotiated worker protections into their AI policies to their own agency's governance planning.

title: Building AI With Your Workforce: Workers as Co-Designers
description: Even with trust and governance in place, many agencies still design and deploy AI tools without ever bringing frontline workers into the actual development process. This closing workshop explores what it looks like to go a step further: treating workers not just as stakeholders to consult, but as co-designers with real influence over how tools are built and implemented. Speakers will share frameworks and examples for involving frontline staff throughout the design and rollout process, so that the resulting tools reflect the realities of the job and the judgment of the people doing it.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Understand the difference between consulting workers and genuinely co-designing AI tools with them.

  • Identify practical methods for involving frontline staff in the design, testing, and rollout of new AI tools.

  • Apply co-design principles to their own agency's AI implementation process, from pilot through full deployment.

title: What aren’t we talking about when we talk about AI
Preparing Communities for Infrastructure Development Conversations
description:
Major infrastructure proposals can raise complex questions about jobs, public services, land use, environmental impacts, energy and water use, aesthetics, and other community priorities. Learn how state and local governments can help residents understand proposed developments and participate meaningfully in conversations and decisions that affect their communities.

Using data centers and other infrastructure projects as examples, explore practical approaches to sharing information, identifying affected communities, gathering local knowledge, surfacing priorities and concerns, and creating opportunities for dialogue before key decisions and commitments are made.

title: From Community Priorities to Agreements
description:
How can community priorities translate into concrete commitments? Learn how community benefit agreements, good neighbor agreements, host community agreements, and related mechanisms are developed, and how responsibilities differ among governments, developers, community organizations, and residents.

Explore how public agencies can support negotiation processes, bring evidence about local conditions and public service needs to the conversation, and help establish commitments that are specific enough to implement and monitor. Examine how continued community participation can strengthen negotiations and help ensure agreements reflect local priorities.

title: From Commitments to Results: Implementation and Accountability
description:
Signing an agreement is only the beginning. Different commitments require different implementation approaches: workforce programs may require coordination among employers, agencies, and training organizations; environmental commitments may require ongoing monitoring; and community funds need clear governance and decision-making processes.

Learn how public agencies and communities can track commitments, communicate progress, respond when expectations are not met, and assess whether promised benefits are producing meaningful results. Explore approaches to maintaining community participation and public transparency throughout project development and operations, including when projects, ownership, or local conditions change.

title: Asking Better Questions: Data Literacy 101
description:
Good data analysis starts with understanding the question you are trying to answer. Learn how to turn everyday public sector challenges into questions that data can help address and identify what information you need to understand a problem, measure progress, or inform a decision.

Through hands-on exercises, explore different types of data, how datasets are structured, and how AI can help you explore data, formulate questions, and identify patterns worth investigating. At the same time, learn to assess whether the data you are working with is relevant, complete, representative, and appropriate to use, including considerations around sensitive information and privacy.

Tool and opportunity: Use data and AI to explore public sector questions and identify potential insights.
Risk and responsibility: Assess whether the underlying data is appropriate, reliable, representative, and safe to use.

title: Making Sense of Data: Statistics, Patterns, and Evidence
description:
You don't need to be a statistician to work effectively with data, but you do need to understand what the numbers can and cannot tell you. Learn how to interpret common statistics, percentages, rates, comparisons, charts, and trends using public sector examples.

Practice using AI to help analyze data, identify patterns, and create visualizations. Learn how to check the results and recognize common problems, including inappropriate comparisons, poor-quality or biased data, confusion between correlation and causation, misleading visualizations, and AI-generated analyses that appear convincing but are not supported by the evidence.

Tool and opportunity: Use AI to support analysis, identify patterns, and visualize data.
Risk and responsibility: Check the data, methods, and AI-assisted analysis before accepting the results or drawing conclusions.

title: From Data to Decisions: Analyzing and Communicating Findings
description:
Working with data ultimately means deciding what the evidence tells you and communicating it in ways that others can understand and use. Learn how to identify meaningful findings, select appropriate visualizations, and translate analysis into clear information for colleagues, decision-makers, and the public.

Practice using AI to support analysis, create visualizations, and develop initial summaries while maintaining responsibility for interpreting and verifying the results. Learn how to communicate uncertainty and limitations, avoid overstating what the data shows, and distinguish between evidence, interpretation, and recommendations.

Tool and opportunity: Use data and AI to develop and communicate evidence-informed findings.
Risk and responsibility: Ensure that conclusions accurately reflect the evidence, limitations and uncertainty are visible, and AI-assisted outputs are independently reviewed before they inform public decisions.

title: From Good Ideas to Actionable Plans
description: As a public manager, you see opportunities to improve how your team works and how services are delivered. But recognizing what needs to change is only the first step. Learn how to define the problem, set clear goals, identify where to start, and develop a realistic plan that fits your team's capacity. Through real government examples, you will learn how to break ideas into manageable steps, involve the right people, and distinguish between changes you can lead directly and those that require support from others.
learning_goals:
• Define a specific problem their team faces and frame a clear, realistic goal for improving it.

  • Break an improvement idea into a small first step that fits their team’s current capacity.

  • Distinguish between changes they can lead directly and those that need support from senior leaders or other parts of the organization.

title: Building Support and Leading Your Team Through Change
description: Leading change requires building support in every direction: with the teams putting improvements into practice, the senior leaders who can help move them forward, and the colleagues whose work may be affected. Learn practical strategies for involving your team early, communicating why a change matters, and making a compelling case to decision-makers. Through real government examples, explore how to understand different perspectives, address concerns constructively, and build the trust, relationships, and shared commitment needed to turn plans into action.
learning_goals:
• Identify ways to involve their team early in shaping a change, so the people putting it into practice help design it.

  • Explain why a change matters in terms that resonate with senior leaders, and outline a brief case for their support.

  • Anticipate concerns from colleagues whose work may be affected, and plan a constructive way to address them.

title: Making Change Happen: From Implementation to Lasting Improvement
description: Even well-planned changes face unexpected challenges once implementation begins. Learn practical approaches to testing improvements on a small scale, assigning responsibilities, tracking progress, and adapting plans based on evidence and feedback. Explore how managers can help their teams navigate setbacks, demonstrate progress to leadership, and integrate new practices into everyday work. Practice identifying meaningful measures of success and developing a plan to sustain improvements that deliver better results for the people you serve.
learning_goals:
• Design a small-scale test of an improvement, with clear owners for each part of the work.

  • Identify one or two meaningful measures of success and use them to track progress and show results to leadership.

  • Outline steps to adjust a plan based on feedback and setbacks, and to build the new practice into the team’s everyday work.

title: Smarter Transit: Using AI for Planning and Operations
description: How can public transportation agencies use AI to deliver more reliable and responsive services? Explore practical applications of AI for predicting passenger demand, optimizing routes and schedules, managing fleets, and anticipating maintenance needs. Drawing on real-world examples, learn how to identify opportunities to use AI in transit operations and planning, assess data requirements, and evaluate potential benefits and limitations.

title: Safer, More Accessible Transit: AI for Passenger Experience
description: Public transportation must be safe, accessible, and responsive to the needs of different passengers. Learn how transit agencies can use AI to support safety monitoring, identify service disruptions, provide real-time passenger information, and improve accessibility. Through practical examples, explore how to assess these applications while addressing privacy, fairness, and the importance of maintaining human oversight.

title: From Pilots to Practice: Implementing AI in Public Transportation
description: Moving from promising AI applications to improvements in public transportation requires careful planning, collaboration, and evaluation. Learn how to identify suitable use cases, assess organizational readiness, and make informed decisions about AI tools and vendors. Explore practical approaches to testing AI applications, engaging frontline staff and passengers, managing implementation risks, and measuring whether AI-supported initiatives deliver meaningful improvements in public transportation.

title: Redesigning Contact Center Operations: People, Workflows, and Coordination
description: Learn how agencies translate modernization goals into changes in everyday contact center operations. Explore practical approaches to workforce planning, redesigning workflows, coordinating services across departments, and preparing frontline staff for new ways of working. Drawing on government experience, identify how operational decisions affect service quality and how to involve staff in designing and implementing improvements.

title: Making Technology Work: Procurement, Integration, and Data Governance
description: Learn how public agencies navigate the technical and procurement decisions involved in modernizing contact centers. Through a detailed government case study, examine how an agency selected technology, worked with vendors, integrated new tools with existing systems, and addressed data privacy and security requirements. Explore the roles of procurement, IT, legal, and operational teams in managing implementation and maintaining accountability.

title: From Implementation to Impact: Managing Change and Measuring Results
description: Learn how to move contact center improvements from initial implementation into everyday operations. Explore approaches to managing organizational change, testing new workflows and technologies, engaging frontline staff, and addressing unexpected challenges. Practice identifying meaningful performance indicators, collecting feedback from residents and employees, and using evidence to improve service delivery over time.

title: Skills: Turning Analysis into Decision-Relevant Information
description:
Quantitative and qualitative analysis does not automatically answer the questions facing state and local governments. Staff must determine which questions to ask, assess the quality of available evidence, examine policy and program alternatives, and communicate tradeoffs.

This session explores how government practitioners use analytical skills to connect evidence with decisions and societal outcomes. Participants will examine how staff assess alternatives using the 4E's: effectiveness, efficiency, equity, and ease of political acceptability.

Speakers could draw on policies and programs involving energy planning, environmental protection, public health, infrastructure, emerging technologies, or economic development. The session will also consider how stories can identify questions that an analysis should address and how community conditions affect the relevance of findings

title: Stories: Connecting Analysis with Lived Experience
description:
Stories can show how people experience a policy, program, investment, or public problem. They can help government staff understand why an issue matters, who benefits, who encounters barriers, and how implementation differs from what aggregate measures suggest.

This session examines how state and local governments collect and interpret stories from residents, program participants, frontline staff, businesses, and community organizations. Participants will consider how stories contribute qualitative evidence that can be analyzed alongside quantitative findings. Speakers will also explore how stories can reveal outcomes, opportunities, or community priorities that existing measures may not capture.

title: Spaces: Localizing Evidence, Action, and Accountability
description:
The same policy or program can produce different results across communities. Infrastructure and institutional capacity shape what can be implemented. Environmental and economic conditions influence the opportunities available, while public trust and previous government decisions affect how communities respond. Together, these conditions help determine who benefits and which challenges remain.

In this framework, spaces are more than meeting places. They include the geographic, institutional, workplace, professional, identity-based, and issue-based communities in which people live, work, organize, and experience the outcomes of government action.

This session examines how government staff connect skills and stories to these settings. Speakers will explore how policies and programs are adapted to local conditions, how governments recognize differences among communities, and how agencies determine whether their actions created meaningful opportunities or addressed important challenges.

title: HR Policy, Labor Partnership, and Workforce Transitions
description: HR performance is defined by policies, partnerships, and the organization’s capability to make critical transitions toward new ways of doing things that reflect current priorities and values.  This session explores how agencies can develop HR policies for responsible AI use that are consistent with merit principles and civil service rules, and why unions and employees need to be partners in those decisions. It also looks at how AI can help agencies plan for succession and capture institutional knowledge when experienced employees retire or move on.  And it examines how AI enables talented employees to develop in ways that reflect shared goals.
learning_goals:
By the end of this workshop, participants will be able to:

  • Identify core elements of a responsible AI use policy for HR that aligns with merit principles and civil service rules.

  • Explain why involving unions and employees early in AI decisions matters, and name at least one way to start that conversation.

  • Describe how AI can support succession planning and help capture institutional knowledge before experienced employees leave.

title: Finding Where AI Fits Your Work
description:
Learn how to identify opportunities to use AI in your daily responsibilities and distinguish between tasks where AI can add value and those where it may not be appropriate. Through guided exercises and public sector examples, identify a practical task you would like to improve.

Practical outcome: Select a real work task to develop throughout the series.

title: Prompting for Better Results: A Step-by-Step Workshop
description:
Practice writing, testing, and refining prompts for common public sector tasks. Learn how to provide context, structure instructions, specify output formats, and improve results through guided exercises using the AI tools available to you.

Practical outcome: Develop and test a reusable prompt for a task you perform regularly.

title: Working with Documents and Information
description:
Learn how to use AI to summarize reports, compare documents, extract relevant information, and prepare initial drafts. Practice step by step with common government materials while learning to preserve context, verify accuracy, and protect sensitive information.

Practical outcome: Develop a reusable approach to a document-intensive task, including steps for checking results.

title: Using AI for Research and Analysis
description:
Practice using AI to formulate research questions, organize evidence, compare sources, and synthesize information. Learn how to verify AI-generated outputs, recognize unsupported claims, and combine AI-assisted analysis with professional judgment to support public sector decisions.

Practical outcome: Prepare a short, evidence-informed analysis of a public sector question.

title: From Individual Prompts to Repeatable Workflows
description:
Move beyond isolated tasks and learn how to integrate AI into recurring work processes. Through guided exercises, practice breaking down a workflow into manageable steps, connecting AI-assisted activities, and identifying where human review and decision-making are essential.

Practical outcome: Design an AI-supported workflow for a recurring task, with clearly defined steps, responsibilities, and safeguards.

title: Testing, Improving, and Sharing What Works
description:
Bring together what you've learned throughout the series to test and refine an AI-supported workflow. Learn how to compare results with your current practices, assess quality and reliability, address limitations, and share effective approaches with colleagues.

Practical outcome: Leave with a tested workflow or implementation plan, including evaluation criteria and next steps for applying it in your work.
